title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 120 (Maintenance and inspection of documents in electronic form)

content.overview: Section 120 permits prescribed company documents and records to be maintained and inspected electronically in the prescribed manner.
content.glance: Electronic maintenance and inspection are permitted only in accordance with the prescribed requirements and rules; the section does not waive the underlying record-keeping duty.
content.study:
## Statutory rule

Section 120 permits documents, records, registers and minutes required to be kept by a company, or available for member inspection, to be maintained and inspected in electronic form in the prescribed manner and subject to the prescribed conditions.

## Practical application

Check whether the record and company fall within the applicable rules; whether access, authentication, integrity, retention and inspection requirements are met; and whether the electronic version is available to the persons legally entitled to inspect it. Preserve reliable records of access and any required copies.

## Relationship with other provisions

Section 120 changes the permitted form of maintenance or inspection; it does not remove the obligation to keep the record, expand inspection rights beyond the Act, or excuse compliance with the provisions governing the particular register, minutes or document.

sections.title: Electronic records
content: Specified company documents, records, registers and minutes may be maintained and inspected electronically in the prescribed manner.
The applicable rules and prescribed conditions determine the practical requirements.

sections.title: Underlying obligations remain
content: Electronic form does not remove the duty to maintain a record or create inspection rights that do not otherwise exist.
Check integrity, retention, access and inspection requirements under the current rules.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What does section 120 permit?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Section 120 permits specified documents, records, registers and minutes to be maintained and inspected in electronic form in the prescribed manner and subject to applicable conditions. The company must still comply with the underlying record-keeping and inspection duties, and should verify the current rules for access, integrity and retention.

examTips: Explain that electronic form is conditional on the prescribed manner.
Distinguish the form of a record from the underlying duty to keep or disclose it.
revisionPoints: Section 120 concerns electronic maintenance and inspection.
Applicable rules and conditions remain important.
Electronic form does not remove underlying statutory duties.
